title: Processes, Signals, and Background Jobs
intro: Finding a process, stopping it politely (or not), and running things that survive after you log out — core skills for any server work.

steps.prompt: Find the PID of any running process named 'worker'.
steps.explanation: pgrep matches by process name and prints just the PIDs.
steps.why: 'ps aux | grep worker' works too, but also matches the grep command itself and prints lots of noise. pgrep gives you exactly the PIDs, ready to pass to kill.

steps.prompt: Ask process 5012 to shut down gracefully.
steps.explanation: Plain kill sends SIGTERM (15), which lets the process finish in-flight work, flush files, and exit cleanly.
steps.why: Always try SIGTERM first. The process gets a chance to clean up — close database connections, finish writing a file. Jumping straight to -9 risks corrupted data.

steps.prompt: Process 5013 is hung and ignores SIGTERM. Force-kill it.
steps.explanation: SIGKILL (9) can't be caught or ignored — the kernel removes the process immediately.
steps.why: -9 is the last resort, not the first move: no cleanup happens at all. It's also why exit code 137 (128+9) in Docker/Kubernetes means 'something force-killed this', usually the OOM killer.

steps.prompt: Start a long-running data migration script so it keeps running even after you disconnect your SSH session.
steps.fake_output:
[1] 6120
nohup: ignoring input and appending output to 'nohup.out'
steps.explanation: nohup ignores the hangup signal sent when your terminal closes; & puts it in the background.
steps.why: Without nohup, closing your laptop kills an hour-long migration halfway through. For anything important, tmux or screen (which let you reattach later) or a proper systemd service are even better options.

steps.prompt: List the background jobs running in your current shell.
steps.explanation: jobs only shows jobs started from THIS shell session.
steps.why: jobs/fg/bg manage your own shell's jobs; for anything system-wide use ps/pgrep. Confusing the two is why 'jobs' shows nothing after you reconnect in a new SSH session.

steps.prompt: A CPU-heavy backup script is slowing down the web server. Lower its priority (PID 7004) so it yields CPU to more important work.
steps.explanation: Higher nice values mean LOWER priority. The backup still runs, it just gets CPU only when others don't need it.
steps.why: Killing the backup loses the work; renice keeps it running without hurting production traffic. To start something at low priority from the beginning, use 'nice -n 10 ./backup.sh' instead.
